title.sourceEnglish: Staple Crops: Maize, Beans, and Root Vegetables
title.tshivendaDraft: Zwimela zwa staple: Maize, Beans, na Root Vegetables

body.sourceEnglish:
A staple earns its place because it feeds the household beyond the day of harvest.

It carries energy or protein. It stores, or it stays in the ground until you need it. And often it carries cultural memory too.

One staple leaves you vulnerable. Two or more give you options when weather or pests hit.

Grow at least two. Not one.

Which staple does your household rely on most heavily right now? That's the one whose failure would hurt most — so that's the one that needs a companion.

Each staple protects you against something different.

Maize gives calories, and stores dry. Open-pollinated maize also lets you save your own seed, if you manage isolation and selection.

Beans and cowpeas give a storable protein harvest.

Sweet potato develops some drought tolerance after its storage roots form. It needs water in the first weeks and while roots are forming; water stress then can reduce the harvest. Its young leaves are edible too.

Amadumbe handles wetter ground, where other staples struggle.

Notice that they fail in different conditions. That's the whole point.

Resilience doesn't mean nothing fails.

It means one failure doesn't finish your household's food plan.

One crop is one point of failure.

Two or more staples give you more ways to keep eating.

Different crops use water, soil and seasons differently. That difference is the protection.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Tshiḽiwa tsha vhuthogwa [staple] tshi wana vhuimo hatsho ngauri tshi ṋea muṱa zwiḽiwa u fhirisa ḓuvha ḽa khaṋo.

Tshiḽiwa tsha vhuthogwa tshi fara energy kana protein. Tshi a vhulungea kana tshi sala tshi mavuni u swika ni tshi tshi ṱoḓa. Nahone kanzhi tshi na cultural memory.

Tshiḽiwa tshithihi tsha vhuthogwa tshi ni sia ni vulnerable. Zwiḽiwa zwa vhuthogwa zwivhili kana zwo engaho zwi ni ṋea khetho musi mutsho kana zwikhokhonono zwi tshi kwama zwimela.

Alusani zwivhili kana zwo engaho. Hu si tshithihi.

Ndi tshiḽiwa tsha vhuthogwa tshifhio tshine muṱa waṋu wa ḓitika ngatsho nga maanḓa u fhira zwiṅwe zwino? Ndi tshone tshine failure yatsho ya vha i tshi ḓo vhaisa vhukuma u fhira zwiṅwe — ngauralo ndi tshone tshine tsha ṱoḓa companion.

Tshiḽiwa tsha vhuthogwa tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe tshi ni tsireledza kha zwithu zwo fhambanaho.

Maize i ṋea calories nahone i a vhulungea yo oma. Open-pollinated maize i dovha ya ni tendela ni vhulunga mbeu yaṋu, arali ni tshi langula isolation na selection.

Beans na cowpeas zwi ṋea protein harvest ine ya nga vhulungwa.

Sweet potato i wana drought tolerance nyana nga murahu ha musi storage roots dza yo dzo no vhumbea. I ṱoḓa maḓi kha vhege dza u thoma na musi storage roots dzi tshi kha ḓi vhumbea; water stress nga tshifhinga tshenetsho i nga fhungudza harvest. young leaves ayo na one a a ḽiwa.

Amadumbe i a konḓelela mavu ane a vha na maḓi manzhi u fhira, hune zwiṅwe zwimela zwa vhuthogwa zwa konḓelwa.

Ṱhogomelani uri zwi kundwa kha conditions dzo fhambanaho. Ndi zwone zwine zwa vha ndeme nga maanḓa.

Resilience a zwi ambi uri a hu na zwine zwa kundwa.

Zwi amba uri u kundwa huṅwe huthihi a hu fhedzi pulane ya zwiḽiwa ya muṱa waṋu.

Tshibyariwa tshithihi ndi point nthihi ya failure.

Zwiḽiwa zwa vhuthogwa zwivhili kana zwo engaho zwi ni ṋea dziṅwe nḓila nnzhi dza u bvela phanḓa ni tshiḽa.

Zwimela zwo fhambanaho zwi shumisa maḓi, mavu na khalaṅwaha nga nḓila dzo fhambanaho. Phambano yeneyo ndi yone tsireledzo.

question.sourceEnglish: Why choose open-pollinated maize over a hybrid variety if you plan to save your own seed?
question.tshivendaDraft: Ndi ngani ni tshi khetha open-pollinated maize u fhira lushaka lwa hybrid arali ni tshi dzudzanya u vhulunga mbeu yaṋu?

options.sourceEnglish: Open-pollinated varieties yield more
options.tshivendaDraft: Varieties dza open-pollinated yield more.

options.sourceEnglish: Hybrid seed won't breed true — the next generation won't match the parent plant
options.tshivendaDraft: Mbeu ya hybrid a i nga ḓo breed true — zwimela zwa murafho u tevhelaho a zwi nga ḓo fana na tshimela tsha mubebi

options.sourceEnglish: Open-pollinated maize is always more drought-tolerant
options.tshivendaDraft: Open-pollinated maize i dzulela u vha more drought-tolerant

options.tshivendaDraft: Hybrids a dzi koni u ṱavhiwa Afurika Tshipembe

rationale.sourceEnglish: Seed saved from an F1 hybrid may grow, but the next generation can vary. A stable open-pollinated variety with managed pollination is more predictable when saving seed.
rationale.tshivendaDraft: Mbeu yo vhulungwaho kha F1 hybrid i nga mela, fhedzi zwimela zwa murafho u tevhelaho zwi nga fhambana. Mvelelo dza lushaka lwa open-pollinated lu re stable lune pollination ya lo ya langwa dzi a leluwa u bvumba u fhira, musi ni tshi vhulunga mbeu.

question.sourceEnglish: Why is amadumbe (taro) a good staple choice for parts of KZN?
question.tshivendaDraft: Ndi ngani amadumbe (taro) i tshi vha khetho yavhuḓi ya staple kha zwiṅwe zwipiḓa zwa KZN?

options.sourceEnglish: It thrives on very dry, sandy soil
options.tshivendaDraft: I aluwa zwavhuḓi kha mavu o omaho vhukuma, a muṱavha

options.tshivendaDraft: A i ṱoḓi cultivation na luthihi

title.tshivendaDraft: U Lugisela na u Ṱavha Beds dzaṋu

infographicAlt.sourceEnglish: A raised bed about 1.2 metres wide, with paths on both sides, so a person can reach the middle from either side without ever standing on the growing soil.
infographicAlt.tshivendaDraft: A raised bed ine ya vha na vhuphara ha about 1.2 metres, i re na paths nga matungo mavhili, uri muthu a swike vhukati a tshi bva kha thungo iṅwe na iṅwe a sa vhuye a ima kha mavu ane a khou limiwa.

body.sourceEnglish:
Compacted soil loses its air spaces. Roots slow down. Water soaks in differently. The bed gets harder to work every season.

The protection is simple. Permanent paths, and a bed narrow enough to reach into from both sides.

One metre to one point two metres wide. That's the working number. At that width you can reach the centre from either path, and your feet never touch the growing area.

Now think about your own beds. Can you reach the middle without stepping inside? Go and try it before you plant anything else.

There's no single bed shape that's right everywhere.

Start with the least disturbance that solves your problem.

No-dig suits most garden soils. Leave the structure alone and build fertility on top.

Do not dig wet clay. If compaction or poor drainage is severe, identify the cause with local advice before choosing deeper cultivation.

Raised beds suit wet ground, where water needs somewhere to drain away to.

Sunken beds suit dry ground, where you want to catch and hold what rain you get.

Look after heavy rain. Where does water sit or run off? Combine that observation with soil and drainage advice before choosing the bed.

Some crops resent having their roots disturbed. They do better sown straight where they'll grow. Beans, carrots and maize belong in that group.

Others do better with a protected start in a nursery, then transplanting. Tomatoes and brassicas belong there.

Use spacing guidance for the crop, variety and local conditions. Check the packet and local grower advice. Watch for crowding as plants develop.

Before you plant, mark the bed out.

One point two metres wide. Three metres long. One practice bed.

Use pegs and string. Mark the rectangle, and mark both access paths.

Then prepare for your own soil — no-dig first, and dig deeper only if your ground genuinely needs it.

A string line turns an idea into a decision. Once the paths exist, keep them. Once the growing area exists, protect it.

That bed gets easier to improve every season, because you stopped walking on it.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Mavu o petetsanaho a xedza zwikhala zwa muya. Midzi i aluwa nga u ongolowa. Maḓi a nwela nga nḓila yo fhambanaho. Bed gets harder to work kha khalaṅwaha iṅwe na iṅwe.

Tsireledzo ndi yo leluwaho. Permanent paths, na bed ine ya vha tsekene lune na nga swikelela nga ngomu ni tshi bva kha masia oṱhe mavhili.

One metre to one point two metres wide. Wonoyo ndi mpimo une wa shumiswa. Kha honoho vhuphara ni nga swikelela vhukati ni tshi bva kha iṅwe na iṅwe ya paths mbili, nahone milenzhe yaṋu a i kwami growing area na luthihi.

Zwino humbulani nga ha beds dzaṋu. Ni nga swikelela vhukati ni sa kande nga ngomu? Iyani ni lingedze zwenezwo ni sa athu ṱavha tshiṅwe tshithu.

A hu na tshivhumbeo tshithihi tsha bed tshine tsha tea fhethu hoṱhe.

Thomani nga least disturbance ine ya tandulula thaidzo yaṋu.

No-dig i tea kha vhunzhi ha mavu a ngade. Litshani structure ya mavu i sa shanduke, nahone ni fhaṱe fertility nga nṱha.

Ni songo bwa wet clay. Arali compaction kana poor drainage zwi tshi vha severe, wanani tshiitisi nga nyeletshedzo ya henefho ni sa athu khetha deeper cultivation.

Raised beds dzi tea wet ground, hune maḓi a ṱoḓa fhethu ha u bva hone.

Sunken beds dzi tea dry ground, hune na ṱoḓa u fara na u vhulunga mvula ine na i wana.

Nga murahu ha mvula khulu, ṱhogomelani. Maḓi a dzula ngafhi kana a elela a bva ngafhi? Ṱanganyisani zwe na vhona na nyeletshedzo nga ha soil and drainage ni sa athu khetha bed.

Zwimela zwiṅwe a zwi takaleli musi midzi yazwo i tshi kavanyedzwa. They do better musi zwi tshi zwaliwa nga ho livhaho hune zwa ḓo aluwa hone. Beans, carrots na maize zwi wela kha tshigwada itsho.

Zwiṅwe zwi ita khwine musi zwi tshi thoma zwo tsireledzea kha nursery, nga murahu transplanting. Tomatoes na brassicas zwi wela henefho.

Shumisani spacing guidance ya crop, variety na local conditions. Sedzani packet na local grower advice. Sedzani crowding musi zwimela zwi tshi aluwa.

Ni sa athu ṱavha, swayani bed.

One point two metres wide. Three metres long. Bed nthihi ya vhuḓowedzi (practice bed).

Shumisani zwipiki na thambo. Swayani rectangle, nahone ni swaye paths dzoṱhe mbili dza u swikelela bed.

Nga murahu ni lugiselele u ya nga mavu aṋu — thomani nga no-dig, nahone ni bwe u tsa fhedzi arali mavu aṋu a tshi zwi ṱoḓa vhukuma.

String line i shandula muhumbulo wa vha tsheo. Musi paths dzi no vha hone, ni dzi litshe dzi dzule hone. Musi growing area i no vha hone, ni i tsireledze.

Bed yeneyo i a leluwa u khwinifhadza khalaṅwaha iṅwe na iṅwe, ngauri no litsha u tshimbila khayo.

keyPoints.sourceEnglish: Crowded plants underperform — space generously for your local climate

question.sourceEnglish: Why keep a vegetable bed to 1-1.2m wide rather than wider?
question.tshivendaDraft: Ndi ngani ni tshi vhulunga bed ya miroho i na vhuphara ha 1-1.2m, nṱhani ha u i ita wider?

options.sourceEnglish: Wider beds get too much sun
options.tshivendaDraft: Beds dzo ṱanḓavhuwaho dzi wana ḓuvha ḽinzhi nga maanḓa

options.sourceEnglish: You can reach the centre from either side without stepping on the growing area, avoiding compaction
options.tshivendaDraft: Ni nga swikelela vhukati ni tshi bva kha ḽiṅwe na ḽiṅwe ḽa masia mavhili ni sa kande fhethu hune zwimela zwa mela, na thivhela compaction.

options.sourceEnglish: Narrow beds drain better in all conditions
options.tshivendaDraft: Narrow beds drain better kha nyimele dzoṱhe

options.sourceEnglish: It's a fixed rule with no practical reason
options.tshivendaDraft: Ndi mulayo wo vhewaho une wa si vha na tshiitisi tsha u shumisa.

rationale.sourceEnglish: Stepping on growing soil compacts it and damages roots — a bed you can reach into from both sides means you never have to.

question.sourceEnglish: Which crop is best suited to direct-seeding rather than transplanting?
question.tshivendaDraft: Ndi tshimela tshifhio tshine tsha vha best suited to direct-seeding rather than transplanting?

options.sourceEnglish: Tomatoes, which need an early start
options.tshivendaDraft: Tomatoes, dzine dza ṱoḓa early start

options.sourceEnglish: Brassicas, which need protection while small
options.tshivendaDraft: Brassicas, dzine dza ṱoḓa tsireledzo musi dzi tshee ṱhukhu

options.sourceEnglish: Beans, which resent root disturbance
options.tshivendaDraft: Beans, dzine dza si takalele root disturbance

options.tshivendaDraft: Peppers, dzine dza ongolowa u mela

rationale.sourceEnglish: Beans and other quick, sensitive-rooted crops establish poorly after transplant shock — sowing them straight into the bed avoids that setback entirely.
rationale.tshivendaDraft: Beans and other quick, sensitive-rooted crops establish poorly nga murahu ha transplant shock — u zwi zwala nga ho livhaho kha bed zwi thivhela setback yeneyo nga hoṱhe.

infographicAlt.sourceEnglish: One bed over three seasons: a fast crop is harvested, then a new sowing goes in beside a slower crop that is still growing, so the bed is never empty.
infographicAlt.tshivendaDraft: Bed nthihi kha khalaṅwaha tharu: tshimela tshine tsha aluwa nga u ṱavhanya tshi a kaṋiwa; nga murahu, hu itwa zwalo ntswa tsini na tshimela tshiṅwe tshine tsha aluwa nga u ongolowa, tshine tsha kha ḓi aluwa, ngauralo bed a i vhuyi ya vha i si na zwimela.

body.sourceEnglish:
Succession planting is a calendar habit, not a special crop.

Choose something your household actually eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, again and again.

Plant a short row every two to three weeks.

Less waste during a glut. Fresh food for longer. And the labour spreads out across the season instead of landing on you all at once.

Separate sowings may reduce the risk of losing everything at once. They do not guarantee a harvest if difficult conditions continue.

Which fast crop could you sow in small batches? Decide on one, and start it this week.

Here's what it looks like in practice.

Sow one. Then two to three weeks later, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

With suitable crop timing, harvests can begin to overlap. The first batch will not always be ready by the fourth sowing.

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Heat may speed things up, or cause a failure.

Watch what your own garden does, and adjust the interval. That observation is the skill.

Intercropping is not just crowding different plants together. Each plant needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The Three Sisters is an example from Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin spreads across the ground, shading the soil and holding moisture.

Timing matters. Establish the maize first, so it's strong enough to carry the beans when they start to climb.

The plants can still compete. Give them suitable space, water and light. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

A household may have a hungry gap: weeks when stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.

Yours might come after stored maize runs out. It might come before winter greens are ready. It might come in a dry period when water limits the garden.

Don't copy somebody else's calendar. Name your own months first.

Write them down. Then choose the crop and the sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That's planning backwards, and it's the difference between a garden that looks productive and a household that eats.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Succession planting ndi maitele a kalenda, hu si tshimela tsho khetheaho.

Nangani tshithu tshine muṱa waṋu wa tshi ḽa kanzhi vhukuma. Nga murahu, sow zwiṱuku zwa tshithu itsho, ni dovhe ni ite tano hafhu na hafhu.

Ṱavhani muduba mupfufhi vhege dziṅwe na dziṅwe dza mbili u swika kha tharu.

U tambisea ha zwiḽiwa hu a fhungudzea musi hu na khaṋo nnzhi. Zwiḽiwa zwiswa zwi a wanala for longer. Na mushumo u a phaḓalala kha khalaṅwaha, u sa ni lemedza woṱhe nga tshifhinga tshithihi.

U ṱavha nga zwifhinga zwo fhambanaho hu nga fhungudza khombo ya u xelelwa nga zwoṱhe nga tshifhinga tshithihi. A zwi khwaṱhisedzi uri ni ḓo wana khaṋo arali nyimele dzi konḓaho dzi tshi bvela phanḓa.

Ndi fast crop ifhio ine na nga sow nga zwipiḓa zwiṱuku? Nangani tshithihi, ni tshi thome ino vhege.

Hezwi ndi zwine zwa itea ngazwo.

Sow tsha u thoma. Nga murahu ha two to three weeks, sow tsha vhuvhili. Nga murahu, sow tsha vhuraru. Nga murahu, sow tsha vhuṋa.

Arali tshifhinga tsha crop tsho tea, khaṋo dzi nga thoma u overlap. A si tshifhinga tshoṱhe tshine tshigwada tsha u thoma tsha vha tsho lugela u kaṋiwa musi ni tshi zwala lwa vhuṋa.

Vhege mbili u swika kha tharu ndi maitele a u thoma, hu si mulayo. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Musi hu tshi fhisa, zwi nga ṱavhanyisa zwithu kana zwa ita uri zwi kundelwe.

Sedzani zwine zwa itea tsimuni yaṋu, ni shandule interval. U sedza nga nḓila iyi ndi yone skill.

U ṱavha zwimela zwo fhambanaho fhethu huthihi a si u tou zwi kuvhanganya fhedzi. Tshimela tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe tshi ṱoḓa mushumo watsho, na fhethu ho eḓanaho uri tshi kone u ita wonoyo mushumo.

The Three Sisters ndi tsumbo ya Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize i ṋea vhulapfu na tshivhumbeo.

Beans dzi gonya maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin i phadalala fhasi, i ita murunzi kha mavu na u vhulunga moisture.

Tshifhinga tshi a vha tsha ndeme. Thomani nga u ita uri maize i khwaṱhe, u itela uri i kone u tikedza beans musi dzi tshi thoma u gonya.

Zwimela zwi nga kha ḓi konkurisana. Ni zwi fhe fhethu ho teaho, maḓi na tshedza. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

Muṱa u nga vha na hungry gap: vhege dzine zwiḽiwa zwo vhulungwaho zwa vha zwi tshi khou fhungudzea phanḓa ha musi khaṋo i tevhelaho i tshi luga.

Hungry gap yaṋu i nga ḓa nga murahu ha musi maize yo vhulungwaho yo fhela. I nga ḓa musi winter greens dzi sa athu u luga. I nga ḓa nga tshifhinga tsho omaho when water limits the garden.

Ni songo kopolola calendar ya muṅwe muthu. Thomani nga u bula miṅwedzi yaṋu.

Iṅwaleni fhasi. Ni kone u khetha crop na sowing date ine ya isa zwiḽiwa kha hungry gap yeneyo.

Hezwi ndi planning backwards, nahone ndi zwone zwi fhambanyisaho garden ine ya vhonala i tshi bveledza na muṱa une wa wana zwiḽiwa.

title.sourceEnglish: Observe and Manage Pests and Disease
title.tshivendaDraft: Sedzani ni lange Pests na Disease.

body.sourceEnglish:
Pest pressure usually rises for a reason.

Plants under stress. One crop dominating the ground. Or broad chemical use that has already removed the predators that were helping you.

So before you treat anything, look at the whole system.

Is the plant short of water? Is the soil compacted, or hungry? Are predators already working on the problem for you?

A yellow leaf is not automatically an insect. It can be water, nutrition, or root damage. Find out which before you act.

Work through four steps, in order.

One. Observe. Look at the damage pattern, the underside of the leaf, the stem, and the plants nearby.

Two. Check for stress. Soil moisture, roots, spacing, nutrition, drainage.

Three. Protect what's helping you. Beneficial insects are doing work you'd otherwise do yourself.

Four. Only then, act — and start with the lightest thing that works. Physical removal, barriers or changes in crop care may help. Check that the action suits the problem and monitor the result.

If a treatment is needed, use a product registered for that crop and pest, and follow its label. This includes neem products. Check protection and harvest waiting instructions. Do not improvise mixtures or stronger doses.

Be honest with yourself about which step you usually skip.

Zwimela zwi re na stress. One crop dominating the ground. Kana broad chemical use yo no bvisa predators dze dza vha dzi tshi ni thusa.

Yellow leaf a i ambi automatically uri ndi insect. Zwenezwo zwi nga vha maḓi, nutrition, kana u vhaisala ha midzi. Wanani uri ndi zwifhio ni sa athu dzhia vhukando.

Tevhelani vhukando vhuṋa nga u tevhekana.

Tsha u thoma. Sedzani. Sedzani damage pattern, tlhelo ḽa fhasi ḽa ḽiṱari, tsinde, na zwimela zwi re tsini.

Tsha vhuvhili. Sedzani stress. Soil moisture, midzi, spacing ya zwimela, nutrition na drainage.

Tsha vhuraru. Tsireledzani zwine zwa khou ni thusa. Beneficial insects (zwikhokhonono zwine zwa thusa) zwi khou ni itela mushumo une na inwi na vha ni tshi ḓo u ita.

Tsha vhuṋa. Ndi hone fhedzi ni tshi dzhia vhukando — thomani nga the lightest thing that works. Physical removal, barriers kana tshanduko kha nḓila ya u ṱhogomela zwimela zwi nga thusa. Ṱolani arali vhukando vhu tshi tea thaidzo, ni bvele phanḓa ni tshi sedza mvelelo.

Ni ḓi ambele ngoho nga ha vhukando vhune na anzela u vhu pfuka.

body.sourceEnglish:
Succession planting is a calendar habit, not a special crop.

Choose something your household actually eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, again and again.

Plant a short row every two to three weeks.

Less waste during a glut. Fresh food for longer. And the labour spreads out across the season instead of landing on you all at once.

Separate sowings may reduce the risk of losing everything at once. They do not guarantee a harvest if difficult conditions continue.

Which fast crop could you sow in small batches? Decide on one, and start it this week.

Here's what it looks like in practice.

Sow one. Then two to three weeks later, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

With suitable crop timing, harvests can begin to overlap. The first batch will not always be ready by the fourth sowing.

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Heat may speed things up, or cause a failure.

Watch what your own garden does, and adjust the interval. That observation is the skill.

Intercropping is not just crowding different plants together. Each plant needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The Three Sisters is an example from Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin spreads across the ground, shading the soil and holding moisture.

Timing matters. Establish the maize first, so it's strong enough to carry the beans when they start to climb.

The plants can still compete. Give them suitable space, water and light. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

A household may have a hungry gap: weeks when stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.

Yours might come after stored maize runs out. It might come before winter greens are ready. It might come in a dry period when water limits the garden.

Don't copy somebody else's calendar. Name your own months first.

Write them down. Then choose the crop and the sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That's planning backwards, and it's the difference between a garden that looks productive and a household that eats.

title.sourceEnglish: Staple Crops: Maize, Beans, and Root Vegetables
title.tshivendaDraft: Zwimela zwa staple: Maize, Beans, na Root Vegetables

body.sourceEnglish:
A staple earns its place because it feeds the household beyond the day of harvest.

It carries energy or protein. It stores, or it stays in the ground until you need it. And often it carries cultural memory too.

One staple leaves you vulnerable. Two or more give you options when weather or pests hit.

Grow at least two. Not one.

Which staple does your household rely on most heavily right now? That's the one whose failure would hurt most — so that's the one that needs a companion.

Each staple protects you against something different.

Maize gives calories, and stores dry. Open-pollinated maize also lets you save your own seed, if you manage isolation and selection.

Beans and cowpeas give a storable protein harvest.

Sweet potato develops some drought tolerance after its storage roots form. It needs water in the first weeks and while roots are forming; water stress then can reduce the harvest. Its young leaves are edible too.

Amadumbe handles wetter ground, where other staples struggle.

Notice that they fail in different conditions. That's the whole point.

Resilience doesn't mean nothing fails.

It means one failure doesn't finish your household's food plan.

One crop is one point of failure.

Two or more staples give you more ways to keep eating.

Different crops use water, soil and seasons differently. That difference is the protection.

infographicAlt.sourceEnglish: A raised bed about 1.2 metres wide, with paths on both sides, so a person can reach the middle from either side without ever standing on the growing soil.
infographicAlt.tshivendaDraft: A raised bed ine ya vha na vhuphara ha about 1.2 metres, i re na paths nga matungo mavhili, uri muthu a swike vhukati a tshi bva kha thungo iṅwe na iṅwe a sa vhuye a ima kha mavu ane a khou limiwa.

body.sourceEnglish:
Compacted soil loses its air spaces. Roots slow down. Water soaks in differently. The bed gets harder to work every season.

The protection is simple. Permanent paths, and a bed narrow enough to reach into from both sides.

One metre to one point two metres wide. That's the working number. At that width you can reach the centre from either path, and your feet never touch the growing area.

Now think about your own beds. Can you reach the middle without stepping inside? Go and try it before you plant anything else.

There's no single bed shape that's right everywhere.

Start with the least disturbance that solves your problem.

No-dig suits most garden soils. Leave the structure alone and build fertility on top.

Do not dig wet clay. If compaction or poor drainage is severe, identify the cause with local advice before choosing deeper cultivation.

Raised beds suit wet ground, where water needs somewhere to drain away to.

Sunken beds suit dry ground, where you want to catch and hold what rain you get.

Look after heavy rain. Where does water sit or run off? Combine that observation with soil and drainage advice before choosing the bed.

Some crops resent having their roots disturbed. They do better sown straight where they'll grow. Beans, carrots and maize belong in that group.

Others do better with a protected start in a nursery, then transplanting. Tomatoes and brassicas belong there.

Use spacing guidance for the crop, variety and local conditions. Check the packet and local grower advice. Watch for crowding as plants develop.

Before you plant, mark the bed out.

One point two metres wide. Three metres long. One practice bed.

Use pegs and string. Mark the rectangle, and mark both access paths.

Then prepare for your own soil — no-dig first, and dig deeper only if your ground genuinely needs it.

A string line turns an idea into a decision. Once the paths exist, keep them. Once the growing area exists, protect it.

That bed gets easier to improve every season, because you stopped walking on it.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Mavu o petetsanaho a xedza zwikhala zwa muya. Midzi i aluwa nga u ongolowa. Maḓi a nwela nga nḓila yo fhambanaho. Bed i a konḓa u shuma khayo khalaṅwaha iṅwe na iṅwe u fhira khalaṅwaha yo fhiraho.

Tsireledzo ndi yo leluwaho. Permanent paths, na bed ine ya vha tsekene lune na nga swikelela nga ngomu ni tshi bva kha masia oṱhe mavhili.

One metre to one point two metres wide. Wonoyo ndi mpimo une wa shumiswa. Kha honoho vhuphara ni nga swikelela vhukati ni tshi bva kha iṅwe na iṅwe ya paths mbili, nahone milenzhe yaṋu a i kwami growing area na luthihi.

Zwino humbulani nga ha beds dzaṋu. Ni nga swikelela vhukati ni sa kande nga ngomu? Iyani ni lingedze zwenezwo ni sa athu ṱavha tshiṅwe tshithu.

A hu na tshivhumbeo tshithihi tsha bed tshine tsha tea fhethu hoṱhe.

Thomani nga least disturbance ine ya tandulula thaidzo yaṋu.

No-dig i tea kha vhunzhi ha mavu a ngade. Litshani structure ya mavu i sa shanduke, nahone ni fhaṱe fertility nga nṱha.

Ni songo bwa wet clay. Arali compaction kana poor drainage zwi tshi vha severe, wanani tshiitisi nga nyeletshedzo ya henefho ni sa athu khetha deeper cultivation.

Raised beds dzi tea wet ground, hune maḓi a ṱoḓa fhethu ha u bva hone.

Sunken beds dzi tea dry ground, hune na ṱoḓa u fara na u vhulunga mvula ine na i wana.

Nga murahu ha mvula khulu, ṱhogomelani. Maḓi a dzula ngafhi kana a elela a bva ngafhi? Ṱanganyisani zwe na vhona na nyeletshedzo nga ha soil and drainage ni sa athu khetha bed.

Zwimela zwiṅwe a zwi takaleli musi midzi yazwo i tshi kavanyedzwa. They do better musi zwi tshi zwaliwa nga ho livhaho hune zwa ḓo aluwa hone. Beans, carrots na maize zwi wela kha tshigwada itsho.

Zwiṅwe zwi ita khwine musi zwi tshi thoma zwo tsireledzea kha nursery, nga murahu transplanting. Tomatoes na brassicas zwi wela henefho.

Shumisani spacing guidance ya crop, variety na local conditions. Sedzani packet na local grower advice. Sedzani crowding musi zwimela zwi tshi aluwa.

Ni sa athu ṱavha, swayani bed.

One point two metres wide. Three metres long. Bed nthihi ya vhuḓowedzi (practice bed).

Shumisani zwipiki na thambo. Swayani rectangle, nahone ni swaye paths dzoṱhe mbili dza u swikelela bed.

Nga murahu ni lugiselele u ya nga mavu aṋu — thomani nga no-dig, nahone ni bwe u tsa fhedzi arali mavu aṋu a tshi zwi ṱoḓa vhukuma.

String line i shandula muhumbulo wa vha tsheo. Musi paths dzi no vha hone, ni dzi litshe dzi dzule hone. Musi growing area i no vha hone, ni i tsireledze.

Bed yeneyo i a leluwa u khwinifhadza khalaṅwaha iṅwe na iṅwe, ngauri no litsha u tshimbila khayo.

body.sourceEnglish:
Succession planting is a calendar habit, not a special crop.

Choose something your household actually eats often. Then sow a small amount of it, again and again.

Plant a short row every two to three weeks.

Less waste during a glut. Fresh food for longer. And the labour spreads out across the season instead of landing on you all at once.

Separate sowings may reduce the risk of losing everything at once. They do not guarantee a harvest if difficult conditions continue.

Which fast crop could you sow in small batches? Decide on one, and start it this week.

Here's what it looks like in practice.

Sow one. Then two to three weeks later, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

With suitable crop timing, harvests can begin to overlap. The first batch will not always be ready by the fourth sowing.

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Heat may speed things up, or cause a failure.

Watch what your own garden does, and adjust the interval. That observation is the skill.

Intercropping is not just crowding different plants together. Each plant needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The Three Sisters is an example from Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin spreads across the ground, shading the soil and holding moisture.

Timing matters. Establish the maize first, so it's strong enough to carry the beans when they start to climb.

The plants can still compete. Give them suitable space, water and light. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

A household may have a hungry gap: weeks when stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.

Yours might come after stored maize runs out. It might come before winter greens are ready. It might come in a dry period when water limits the garden.

Don't copy somebody else's calendar. Name your own months first.

Write them down. Then choose the crop and the sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That's planning backwards, and it's the difference between a garden that looks productive and a household that eats.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Succession planting ndi maitele a kalenda, hu si tshimela tsho khetheaho.

Nangani tshithu tshine muṱa waṋu wa tshi ḽa kanzhi vhukuma. Nga murahu, sow zwiṱuku zwa tshithu itsho, ni dovhe ni ite tano hafhu na hafhu.

Ṱavhani muduba mupfufhi vhege dziṅwe na dziṅwe dza mbili u swika kha tharu.

U tambisea ha zwiḽiwa hu a fhungudzea musi hu na khaṋo nnzhi. Zwiḽiwa zwiswa zwi a wanala for longer. Na mushumo u a phaḓalala kha khalaṅwaha, u sa ni lemedza woṱhe nga tshifhinga tshithihi.

U ṱavha nga zwifhinga zwo fhambanaho hu nga fhungudza khombo ya u xelelwa nga zwoṱhe nga tshifhinga tshithihi. A zwi khwaṱhisedzi uri ni ḓo wana khaṋo arali nyimele dzi konḓaho dzi tshi bvela phanḓa.

Ndi fast crop ifhio ine na nga sow nga zwipiḓa zwiṱuku? Nangani tshithihi, ni tshi thome ino vhege.

Hezwi ndi zwine zwa itea ngazwo.

Sow tsha u thoma. Nga murahu ha two to three weeks, sow tsha vhuvhili. Nga murahu, sow tsha vhuraru. Nga murahu, sow tsha vhuṋa.

Arali tshifhinga tsha crop tsho tea, khaṋo dzi nga thoma u overlap. A si tshifhinga tshoṱhe tshine tshigwada tsha u thoma tsha vha tsho lugela u kaṋiwa musi ni tshi zwala lwa vhuṋa.

Vhege mbili u swika kha tharu ndi maitele a u thoma, hu si mulayo. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Musi hu tshi fhisa, zwi nga ṱavhanyisa zwithu kana zwa ita uri zwi kundelwe.

Sedzani zwine zwa itea tsimuni yaṋu, ni shandule interval. U sedza nga nḓila iyi ndi yone skill.

U ṱavha zwimela zwo fhambanaho fhethu huthihi a si u tou zwi kuvhanganya fhedzi. Tshimela tshiṅwe na tshiṅwe tshi ṱoḓa mushumo watsho, na fhethu ho eḓanaho uri tshi kone u ita wonoyo mushumo.

The Three Sisters ndi tsumbo ya Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize i ṋea vhulapfu na tshivhumbeo.

Beans dzi gonya maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin i phadalala fhasi, i ita murunzi kha mavu na u vhulunga moisture.

Tshifhinga tshi a vha tsha ndeme. Thomani nga u ita uri maize i khwaṱhe, u itela uri i kone u tikedza beans musi dzi tshi thoma u gonya.

Zwimela zwi nga kha ḓi konkurisana. Ni zwi fhe fhethu ho teaho, maḓi na tshedza. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

Muṱa u nga vha na hungry gap: vhege dzine zwiḽiwa zwo vhulungwaho zwa vha zwi tshi khou fhungudzea phanḓa ha musi khaṋo i tevhelaho i tshi luga.

Hungry gap yaṋu i nga ḓa nga murahu ha musi maize yo vhulungwaho yo fhela. I nga ḓa musi winter greens dzi sa athu u luga. I nga ḓa nga tshifhinga tsho omaho musi maḓi a tshi fhungudza zwine zwa nga aluswa tsimuni.

Ni songo kopolola calendar ya muṅwe muthu. Thomani nga u bula miṅwedzi yaṋu.

Iṅwaleni fhasi. Ni kone u khetha crop na sowing date ine ya isa zwiḽiwa kha hungry gap yeneyo.

Hezwi ndi planning backwards, nahone ndi zwone zwi fhambanyisaho garden ine ya vhonala i tshi bveledza na muṱa une wa wana zwiḽiwa.

title.sourceEnglish: Observe and Manage Pests and Disease
title.tshivendaDraft: Sedzani ni lange Pests na Disease.

infographicAlt.sourceEnglish: A pest on a leaf, and three ways to deal with it without chemicals: a beneficial insect, a physical barrier, and picking it off by hand.
infographicAlt.tshivendaDraft: Pest kha ṱari, na nḓila tharu dza u i langa hu si na chemicals: beneficial insect, physical barrier, na u i bvisa nga tshanḓa.

body.sourceEnglish:
Pest pressure usually rises for a reason.

Plants under stress. One crop dominating the ground. Or broad chemical use that has already removed the predators that were helping you.

So before you treat anything, look at the whole system.

Is the plant short of water? Is the soil compacted, or hungry? Are predators already working on the problem for you?

A yellow leaf is not automatically an insect. It can be water, nutrition, or root damage. Find out which before you act.

Work through four steps, in order.

One. Observe. Look at the damage pattern, the underside of the leaf, the stem, and the plants nearby.

Two. Check for stress. Soil moisture, roots, spacing, nutrition, drainage.

Three. Protect what's helping you. Beneficial insects are doing work you'd otherwise do yourself.

Four. Only then, act — and start with the lightest thing that works. Physical removal, barriers or changes in crop care may help. Check that the action suits the problem and monitor the result.

If a treatment is needed, use a product registered for that crop and pest, and follow its label. This includes neem products. Check protection and harvest waiting instructions. Do not improvise mixtures or stronger doses.

Be honest with yourself about which step you usually skip.
body.tshivendaDraft:
Pest pressure i anzela u engedzea nga tshiitisi.

Zwimela zwi re na stress. One crop dominating the ground. Kana broad chemical use yo no bvisa predators dze dza vha dzi tshi ni thusa.

Ngazwenezwo, ni sa athu u thoma u lafha tshithu, sedzani system yoṱhe.

Naa tshimela tshi khou shaya maḓi? Mavu o compacted kana a si na pfushi? Predators dzi khou shuma kha thaidzo iyi dzi tshi ni thusa already naa?

Yellow leaf a i ambi automatically uri ndi insect. Zwenezwo zwi nga vha maḓi, nutrition, kana u vhaisala ha midzi. Wanani uri ndi zwifhio ni sa athu dzhia vhukando.

Tevhelani vhukando vhuṋa nga u tevhekana.

Tsha u thoma. Sedzani. Sedzani damage pattern, tlhelo ḽa fhasi ḽa ḽiṱari, tsinde, na zwimela zwi re tsini.

Tsha vhuvhili. Sedzani stress. Soil moisture, midzi, spacing ya zwimela, nutrition na drainage.

Tsha vhuraru. Tsireledzani zwine zwa khou ni thusa. Beneficial insects (zwikhokhonono zwine zwa thusa) zwi khou ni itela mushumo une na inwi na vha ni tshi ḓo u ita.

Tsha vhuṋa. Ndi hone fhedzi ni tshi dzhia vhukando — thomani nga the lightest thing that works. Physical removal, barriers kana tshanduko kha nḓila ya u ṱhogomela zwimela zwi nga thusa. Ṱolani arali vhukando vhu tshi tea thaidzo, ni bvele phanḓa ni tshi sedza mvelelo.

Arali treatment i tshi ṱoḓea, shumisani product registered for that crop and pest, nahone ni tevhele label yayo. Hezwi zwi katela neem products. Ṱolani protection and harvest waiting instructions. Ni songo ḓiitela misanganedzo kana stronger doses.

Ni ḓi ambele ngoho nga ha vhukando vhune na anzela u vhu pfuka.

Separate sowings may reduce the risk of losing everything at once. They do not guarantee a harvest if difficult conditions continue.

Which fast crop could you sow in small batches? Decide on one, and start it this week.

Here's what it looks like in practice.

Sow one. Then two to three weeks later, sow two. Then sow three. Then sow four.

With suitable crop timing, harvests can begin to overlap. The first batch will not always be ready by the fourth sowing.

Two to three weeks is a starting rhythm, not a law. A cool-season leaf crop may hold longer. Heat may speed things up, or cause a failure.

Watch what your own garden does, and adjust the interval. That observation is the skill.

Intercropping is not just crowding different plants together. Each plant needs a job, and enough space to do it.

The Three Sisters is an example from Indigenous farming traditions in the Americas.

Maize gives height and structure.

Beans climb the maize, and store as protein.

Pumpkin spreads across the ground, shading the soil and holding moisture.

Timing matters. Establish the maize first, so it's strong enough to carry the beans when they start to climb.

The plants can still compete. Give them suitable space, water and light. Beans fix nitrogen with root bacteria, but do not assume they immediately feed the maize; nutrients in residues are released during decomposition.

A household may have a hungry gap: weeks when stored food runs low before the next harvest is ready.

Yours might come after stored maize runs out. It might come before winter greens are ready. It might come in a dry period when water limits the garden.

Don't copy somebody else's calendar. Name your own months first.

Write them down. Then choose the crop and the sowing date that puts food into that gap.

That's planning backwards, and it's the difference between a garden that looks productive and a household that eats.
